title: Don't Call It a Ban. Call It a Delay.
author: Martinko, Katherine
summary: Katherine Martinko responds to Canada's Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, arguing that critics are holding the legislation to an impossible standard of perfection rather than celebrating genuine progress. Australia's first four months of its under-16 social media ban produced a 37% reduction in account holders, which critics call failure; Martinko argues that if 20% population adoption suffices to shift social norms, even this partial uptake is a real win. Australia's eSafety Commissioner coined a more useful framing—calling the law a 'delay' rather than a 'ban'—because delay implies temporary collective protection rather than prohibition, and is more likely to build cultural consensus. Martinko amplifies Jonathan Haidt's distinction between algorithmically driven social media platforms and general internet use, emphasizing that advocates seek to restrict only the specific tools proven harmful and prone to compulsion. She closes by observing that a national delay primarily validates the minority of parents already choosing low-tech childhoods and gives their children social cover to opt out.
points: Canada's Bill C-34 joins a global wave—Spain, Norway, Sweden, Indonesia, and others—limiting child access to social media and AI chatbots, with 75% of Canadians supporting it in a March 2026 poll.
Australia's first four months of its under-16 ban produced a 37% reduction in under-16 account holders; at 20% adoption required to shift social norms, even imperfect compliance counts as progress.
Language matters: calling legislation a 'delay' rather than a 'ban' signals temporary collective protection rather than permanent prohibition, and is strategically more likely to build broad support.

Jonathan Haidt's framing is useful: advocates are not against the internet broadly but against specific algorithmically driven platforms proven harmful and prone to compulsive use—the distinction matters for public messaging.
National legislation's most important benefit may be validating parents already choosing low-tech childhoods and providing their children social cover to opt out without feeling like outliers.
quotes: many people are contemptuous, citing the fact that non-compliance rates are high and, as of April, only one quarter of 14- and 15-year-olds had stopped using social media. Data from the country's e-Safety commissioner indicated a 37 percent reduction in under-16s holding accounts in the first four months of the ban.

it is said that roughly 20% of a population must change its practices in order to alter social norms, which means that, given time, even at relatively low uptake rates, the necessary shift will occur.

What you’re effectively asking us to do with this is fence the ocean. We might be able to create some friction and some degree of safety, but it’s a futile exercise if you think you’re totally stemming the ocean.

Bans are generally not received well by people who instinctively don’t like being told what to do. Delay has a softer undertone; it suggests a temporary need for the collective protection of our children and youth
we’re not trying to block kids from the Internet, but rather from specific algorithmically driven platforms (namely social media) that have been shown to be harmful and prone to compulsive use.
To choose inaction, knowing what we know about social media’s effects on young brains, would be negligent.

Implementing an official national delay on social media access will, at the very least, reinforce and validate the efforts of parents who do want to preserve their kids’ experience of analog childhood for as long as possible
